There is also provision for situations in which performance is required urgently. 
In a procedure for interim relief known as référé, where the existence of an obliga­
tion is beyond serious question, a juge des référés can order the defaulting party to 
perform, even before finally determining the case. For positive obligations, there is 
a special kind of référé, called the référé-​injonction de faire.81
(d)  The reasons for the wide availability of specific enforcement
A range of justifications have been advanced for the wide availability of specific en­
forcement. The first is the binding force of contract (principe de la force obligatoire 
du contrat) or pacta sunt servanda, meaning that one must perform that which one 
has promised.82 The bond created by the voluntary will of the parties can only be 
given full effect by remedies that compel performance.83
It is also often argued that the preference in France for specific enforcement is 
partly attributable to a perception that damages are an inferior remedy for breach 
of contract.84 They subvert the principle that contractual obligations have binding 
force and, by their nature, are incapable of providing the injured party with full 
satisfaction or fulfilment of their expectations. These deficiencies inevitably follow 
from the acceptance, tacit in any award of damages, that the injured party will not 
receive the promised performance.85 This is portrayed as a ‘favour’ to the contract-​
breaker, and damages as an unsatisfactory stopgap for the injured party.86
Specific enforcement is also argued to reinforce transactional security. To prefer 
damages over compelling performance is for many French commentators tanta­
mount to making obligations optional. Specific enforcement promotes trust be­
tween contracting parties and in the market more broadly. It is essential for the 
orderly functioning of the economy that ‘promises [are] kept’.87
